Turf around a Haines City pool cage

There's no separate price key for pool turf: a Haines City lanai job falls under the residential range, $8–$18 a square foot, generally toward the top half once glue-down edges and drainage are factored in. A screen enclosure built on regraded ridge ground needs a drainage underlay where turf meets the deck, and a lot near one of the city's ridge lakes may also sit inside the state's ten-foot waterbody line.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Turfing a narrow strip inside a screen enclosure

Picture a 210 sq ft ribbon of grass wrapping the inside of a screen enclosure on a lot backing onto one of Haines City's smaller ridge lakes, with the deck itself taking up most of the remaining pad. Multiplying that footprint by the residential range, $8–$18 a square foot, puts the job somewhere between $1,680 and $3,780, though a cramped enclosure job like this one usually settles closer to $3,360 than to the bottom of that span, since a glue-down deck edge and a drainage underlay both add labor a wide-open lawn never needs. The lake behind the cage only changes that math if turf is also going into the open yard beyond the screen, inside the ten-foot line.

A pool cage backing onto a ridge lake

A pool enclosure on a Haines City lot that backs onto Lake Eva or one of the smaller ridge lakes nearby sits closer to the state's ten-foot waterbody setback than most homeowners expect, since a screened lanai's outer edge can run surprisingly close to a property's water frontage on a narrower ridge lot. Turf inside the enclosure itself is unaffected by that setback, which only governs the strip of yard actually within ten feet of the water; it's the open ground between the cage and the lake, if there is any left to turf, that has to respect the line unless a seawall already separates the two.

What does a small deck border cost, worked out?

Installed turf runs eight to eighteen dollars a square foot, typically ten to sixteen, and price does not change by Haines City ZIP code, only by access, base condition, and drainage. Say a homeowner wants a 250 sq ft strip between the pool cage and a side fence turfed rather than reseeded: at the typical range, that job runs somewhere between roughly twenty-five hundred and four thousand dollars, before accounting for anything unusual about the site. A quote well outside that range for a plain open border, high or low, is worth asking about specifically, since the underlying material and labor do not vary by neighborhood.

Grading a pool deck on sloped ridge ground

A pool built on a lot regraded from former grove land doesn't always sit on perfectly level ridge sand the way an older, undisturbed lot might, and a deck feathered against a slight grade change needs the turf's base built to match that same taper rather than assuming a flat plane. Right where the lawn stops and the pool deck's slab starts, glue takes over from nails, simply because there's no dirt left at that exact line for a fastener to bite into once the concrete begins.

Why the ground near the pump pad stays wetter than the rest of the yard

The equipment pad next to a pool, where the pump and filter sit, sheds backwash and drips more consistently than any other spot on a Haines City lot, and turf bordering that pad needs the same washed rock depth and undisturbed native sand as anywhere else to keep that extra moisture moving down instead of sitting at the surface. Compacting the soil under that section too hard, which is easy to do when equipment traffic has already packed it down over the years, works against the percolation the state's turf standard requires. A border here often needs a fresh pass of loosening before rock goes down.

Bare feet and hot turf between the loungers and the water

Full summer sun pushes turf surface temperature to 120 to 150°F, and the stretch of turf between a set of pool loungers and the water in Haines City sees more bare feet crossing it in an afternoon than almost anywhere else on the property. A hose rinse drops that temperature 30 to 50 degrees within minutes, which matters more here than on a side yard nobody walks barefoot across. Timing pool time for morning or late afternoon in peak summer, or rinsing the crossing points before anyone gets in the water, does more for comfort than any product choice does on its own.

Why does coping get a different anchor than a fence line?

The state's turf standard requires edges anchored against wind and flooding, but how that anchoring happens changes at a Haines City pool: along a fence line, the perimeter still takes nails or a bender-board edge into soil the way any residential border would, while along the coping itself, the edge bonds with adhesive into the hard trim rather than being pinned into anything soft. Mixing the two methods up, nailing into coping or trying to glue a soft fence-line edge, leaves a section that either cannot hold or cracks the material it is anchored into within a season.

Rechecking a septic lid's clearance years after a pool project

A septic lid marked and protected during a Haines City pool-area turf build is worth rechecking periodically in the years afterward, since new landscaping, a stored pool float, or equipment added near the pump pad over time can gradually encroach on a spot nobody's paying close attention to anymore. Confirming the lid is still visible and clear takes only a minute during any other routine check of the border or lanai floor, and it's far easier than rediscovering the location from scratch the day a pump-out truck actually needs it. This matters most on properties where the original construction notes have long since been forgotten.

Why a newer enclosure lot needs a different underlay plan

Haines City's newer pool-home subdivisions, many of them built where citrus rows used to run, sit on fill rather than native ridge sand inside the screen enclosure, and that fill can hold water against the concrete deck differently than undisturbed Candler sand would. A drainage underlay beneath the turf gives that trapped moisture somewhere to go besides sitting against the slab, which matters more on a recently graded lot than on an older enclosure built directly over sand that's been settling for decades already.

Questions people ask

Does the ten-foot waterbody setback apply inside a screened pool cage?

No. The setback governs open yard within ten feet of a pond, lake or canal; turf inside an already-screened enclosure isn't the part of the property the rule is written for, since the enclosure itself isn't waterfront ground being newly turfed.

Why does turf near a Haines City pool sometimes cost more per square foot than a plain backyard?

Small, enclosed areas take proportionally more labor for the same crew and equipment mobilization, and a glue-down edge against a concrete deck plus a drainage underlay both add steps a flat, open backyard skips entirely.
